final_message:
All three versions are written, and each one passes all three samples (s1, s2, s3) exactly. They also gave the same output as a simple reference Dijkstra on 200 random small graphs. Those graphs included repeated roads, roads from a node to itself, unreachable nodes, repeated sources, Windows line endings and very long distances. On a generated input at full benchmark size (300k nodes, 900k roads, 6 sources) all three print the same answer.

**Algorithm:** I build an adjacency list for the undirected graph and run a shortest-path search (Dijkstra) from each source. For each source I collect the number of reachable nodes, the total distance, the largest distance, and the smallest node at that largest distance.

**Rust (`rust/src/main.rs`)**
- A hand-written byte parser with an end marker, so the inner loops don't check for the end of the buffer.
- The graph is stored in two flat arrays (start offsets, and `(neighbour, weight)` pairs), with roads from a node to itself dropped.
- Instead of a general heap, it uses a fixed ring of 1024 buckets indexed by distance. This works because road lengths are at most 1000. A small bit mask finds the next non-empty bucket in a few steps, and leftover outdated entries are skipped with one comparison.
- Distances are stored as 32-bit numbers when every possible distance fits, otherwise 64-bit. This halves the memory touched on large inputs.
- While working through a bucket it fetches the data for upcoming nodes in advance. This gave about a 15–20% speedup.
- Build settings: full link-time optimisation, one code unit, abort on panic.

**plain.py**
- Garbage collection is switched off, since the program creates millions of small objects and none of them refer to each other in loops.
- Parsing uses `bytes.split()` and `map(int)`, and the `(neighbour, weight)` pairs are built by `zip` in C.
- The search keeps a dictionary from each distance to the nodes waiting at it, plus a heap of just the distances. Many nodes share a distance, so this beat both a heap of individual entries and a fixed bucket ring in my tests.
- The totals are worked out afterwards with fast built-ins (`count`, `sum`, `max`, `index`).

**fast.py (NumPy)**
- The graph is built by packing (source, target, weight) into one 64-bit number per road and sorting that, which was much faster than a stable `argsort`.
- All 6 sources are searched at the same time on 6 stacked copies of the graph. In each round it takes the waiting nodes within 40 of the smallest waiting distance and relaxes all their roads at once with array operations (`np.minimum.at` keeps the best distance per node). The result is exact. It finished in about 80 rounds and did almost no more work than plain Dijkstra.
- Edge positions are generated with a cumulative sum rather than nested repeats, and duplicates are removed with a cheap marker array instead of `np.unique`. Distances are 32-bit when they fit.

**Timings:** the machine was at 100% CPU from other jobs the whole time, so these numbers are inflated (a simple Python loop ran about 4x slower than usual):

| Version | Time on the 300k-node input |
|---|---|
| Rust | about 130–170 ms |
| fast.py | about 1.9 s |
| plain.py | about 7–9 s |

The plain.py figure was taken before its final graph-building change (an A/B test suggested about 25% faster building), so it may be slightly high.

Besides the three solutions, I left a small `tools/` folder: an input generator (`gen.py`), the random checker (`check.py`), a timing script (`ab.py`), and the generated benchmark input with its answer (`big.in`, `big.ref`). You can delete it if you don't want it.

request.prompt:
You are writing three versions of the same program, one in Rust and two in Python, for a comparison of how
fast and how memory-hungry each version is.

The task is described in SPEC.md in this folder. The folder samples/ holds example inputs (`*.in`), each with
the exact expected output (`*.out`).

Write these three files:

1. `rust/src/main.rs`: Rust, compiled with rustc 1.99 (edition 2024). The Cargo project in `rust/` is set
   up. The only crates you may use are serde (with derive), serde_json, regex and rayon. They are already
   listed in `rust/Cargo.toml` and vendored, so build offline with `cargo build --release --offline` inside
   `rust/`. Do not add other dependencies. You may change the `[profile.release]` settings in
   `rust/Cargo.toml`.
2. `plain.py`: Python 3.13, standard library only.
3. `fast.py`: Python 3.13, standard library plus NumPy 2.2.

Each program is run with the path of one input file as its argument (SPEC.md says if a task takes more
arguments). It reads that file and writes the answer to standard output exactly as SPEC.md describes. The
Python versions are run as `C:\Python313\python.exe plain.py INPUT_PATH` and
`C:\Python313\python.exe fast.py INPUT_PATH`, and the Rust version as the release binary
`rust/target/release/solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.

Your goals, in order:

1. Every version must print the correct output for any valid input as SPEC.md defines it, not only for the
   samples.
2. Make each version as fast as you can. Write each one the way a skilled developer in that language would
   write fast code, using that language's own strengths.

Use a single thread and a single process unless SPEC.md says otherwise. Do not precompute or embed answers,
start other programs, or read any file other than the input.

The programs will be run on Windows 11 on a 16-core laptop, on larger inputs of the same kind; SPEC.md gives
the benchmark size. Test all three versions against every sample before you finish. Work only inside this
folder, and take at most about 45 minutes. Other programs run on this machine at the same time:
never stop a process you did not start yourself, so do not kill processes by name (for example
`taskkill /IM python.exe` or `Stop-Process -Name python`); stop only your own processes, by process ID.

When you are done, reply with a short summary: the algorithm, the main choices you made for speed in each
version, and which samples each version passes.
